newsitem.title: USA: Radiation fights recurrence in early breast cancer.
newsitem.headline: Radiation fights recurrence in early breast cancer.

text.p: Women with early stage breast cancer who have radiation after surgery are less likely to have a recurrence than those who do not, but there is no difference in overall survival, a new study said on Tuesday.

The study of 837 women in Wednesday's Journal of the National Cancer Institute updates research that followed the patients for nearly four years. Now, they have been followed for a median of 7.6 years.
The study of women who had early breast cancer with no lymph node involvement was conducted by Dr. Roy Clark and colleagues at the Ontario Clinical Oncology Group in Canada.

Three times as many women who did not have radiation had recurrent cancers in the breast, but differences in mortality were narrower -- 24 percent, or 99, women who did not have radiation, compared to 21 percent, or 87 women, who did have radiation. Other studies have reached similar conclusions.
Age of the patient and the size and condition of the tumour were considered important prognostic factors.
"The fact that radiation reduced the risk of local recurrence but did not appear to affect overall survival remains difficult to explain," the authors wrote.
